newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Ousland follows countryman to history on Antarctic.
newsitem.headline: Ousland follows countryman to history on Antarctic.

text.p: Norwegian explorer Borge Ousland followed in his countryman's footsteps when he became the first person to walk across Antarctica alone and unaided, arriving at New Zealand's Scott Base on Saturday.

At times retracing the route taken by Roald Amundsen, the first person to reach the South Pole in 1911, Ousland travelled 1,800 miles (2,880 km) across the vast Antarctic continent's perilous terrain in the longest solo polar trek ever accomplished.
"I feel like I'm born again," an exhausted Ousland told Reuters after completing his historic journey. "It's so great to finally accomplish the goal."
Ousland, 34, arrived at Scott Base on the Pacific coast of Antarctica at about 1 p.m. (0000 GMT), two months after he set out from Berkner Island in the Weddell Sea on November 15.
Dragging a 165 kg (396 lb) sled with provisions, he used skis and a giant "para-wing" sail to speed his journey across the world's coldest continent.
Ousland said the temperature had sometimes fallen to minus 45 degrees Celsius and blizzard conditions had often blinded him as he negotiated the frozen landscape, riddled with crevasses.
"I remember on the second day there was a storm and the tent doors blew away and I was wondering 'What am I doing here? How could I be so stupid?'," he said.

"But the scenery out here, it's very beautiful, that's one of the reasons why I do this. It's untouched more or less by humans. I get closer to nature and through the struggle, I also get closer to myself."
Ousland said one of his most memorable moments was following Amundsen's descent from the South Polar Plateau.

"It was the same route that Roald Amundsen took and when I got down, I could see the Ross ice shelf stretching out. Then I knew I had most of the difficult part behind me and now it was a flat stretch to Scott Base," he said.

One of the world's most experienced polar explorers, Ousland had already become the first person to reach both of the Earth's poles alone without the aid of dogs, motorised transport or air-dropped provisions.

He reached the North Pole on April 22, 1994, after 52 days alone and on foot. On December 21 1995, during his first attempt to cross Antarctica, he completed a trek of 825 miles (1,325 km) to the South Pole before frostbite forced him to give up.

"Antarctica is I think a much more mental challenge. You might say that the Arctic is the fear of the unpredictable because you have the shifting ice, everything is moving and you fall in the water and there are polar bears," he said.
In achieving the first and only unsupported crossing of Antarctica, Ousland said he felt he had made history, as Amundsen had before him.
But the richest rewards came from his own experiences on the polar ice-cap.
"You really know and feel that nature is the strongest here, and as a human you feel extremely vulnerable and extremely small. That's a very good feeling to have and to carry with you," he said.
